answer:
**Each bootstrap tree gets its own temporary holdout.** A bootstrap sample draws N times with replacement from N rows. On any draw, one particular row is missed with probability 1-1/N. Missing it on every draw has probability $(1-1/N)^N$. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

Take logarithms: $\log[(1-1/N)^N]=N\log(1-1/N)$. Since log(1-z) is approximately -z for small z, this approaches -1, so the probability approaches $e^{-1}\approx0.368$.

For a given training row, aggregate predictions only from trees that did not sample it. Those are its out-of-bag predictions. Different rows use different tree subsets; there is not one permanent 36.8% holdout shared by the forest.

**Respect dependence and model selection.** OOB can be useful for ordinary independently sampled data, but it does not simulate forecasting into the future or predicting unseen groups when related examples remain in training. Repeatedly tuning to OOB results can also overfit that estimate. Keep a deployment-appropriate final evaluation split for the whole modeling process.

**Technical details and references.**

A bootstrap sample draws $N$ times with replacement from $N$ rows. A particular row is omitted with probability $(1-1/N)^N$, which tends to $e^{-1}$ because $N\log(1-1/N)\to-1$. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html)

OOB prediction for a row averages only trees that did not train on it, giving an internal validation estimate. It is not a substitute for a temporal/group holdout when examples are dependent, and repeatedly tuning to OOB results can introduce selection bias. The 36.8% figure is per tree in expectation, not a fixed permanently held-out subset shared by all trees.
